claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim “safety-relevant representations are not eliminated but bypassed, with only a small subset of attention heads suppressed,” run paired representational and circuit-discovery analyses on at least two open safety-aligned checkpoints, such as Llama-2-7B-Chat and Llama-2-13B-Chat. Use harmful instructions from the public AdvBench and JailbreakBench datasets, generate GCG and standard template jailbreaks, and retain same-instruction pairs in which the ordinary prompt is refused but the jailbreak succeeds under deterministic decoding. Calibrate the success judge against human labels before analysis. Record every head’s output, norm, and projection onto harmfulness and refusal directions for ordinary harmful prompts, successful jailbreaks, failed jailbreaks, and benign Alpaca controls. Train diagnostic probes only on ordinary harmful-versus-benign examples and test them, without refitting, on successful jailbreak activations; this tests whether harmful-content information persists out of distribution. In parallel, use ACDC, attribution patching, and HISP with sparsity sweeps to identify heads whose safety-related output is consistently reduced specifically during successful attacks. Require a quantitatively small set, stability across attacks and data splits, and stronger suppression than size-matched random or activation-magnitude-matched heads. Persistence of cross-condition probe accuracy in most heads, alongside concentrated suppression of a small refusal-associated subset, would support bypass rather than representational erasure; broad loss of decodability would support elimination, while diffuse changes would reject the selective-suppression claim. Replication across checkpoints would strengthen generality, whereas inconsistent head identities but consistent functional roles would support only a functional, not anatomical, version of the claim. This experiment could be reduced or skipped if public paired clean/jailbroken activation traces with independently validated success labels and full per-head measurements already existed for the same checkpoints and benchmarks.

To address subclaim “suppressing the identified subset of attention heads is sufficient to turn refusal into compliance,” intervene on the heads selected using only the discovery split from the first experiment. On held-out AdvBench and JailbreakBench instructions that the unmodified model refuses, scale those head outputs through w ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2} at every relevant prompt and generation position, and separately patch in the head values observed during the matched successful jailbreak. Measure refusal rate, policy-relevant compliance, response relevance, and output KL under deterministic decoding, using a human-calibrated judge. Test the reverse intervention as well: during an actual jailbreak, patch the selected heads from the matched ordinary refused run or amplify them, asking whether refusal is restored. Include unmodified inference, size- and layer-matched random heads, globally high-magnitude heads, failed-jailbreak pairs, and benign Alpaca prompts; measure benign instruction-following and general output degradation so that indiscriminate model damage cannot masquerade as a safety effect. A large, dose-dependent rise in relevant harmful compliance from suppressing only the selected heads, together with restoration of refusal when their clean activations are patched back, would provide evidence for causal sufficiency and a bypass mechanism. An effect no larger than random ablation, an effect requiring many heads, or broad degradation on benign prompts would refute or substantially narrow the claim. Existing public intervention results would make this unnecessary only if they include held-out causal ablations, reverse patching, random-head controls, benign-task controls, and human-validated compliance labels rather than correlational activation measurements alone.

To address subclaim “the persistent representations can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, without additional training, at quality competitive with dedicated safety models,” freeze the checkpoints, layers, and persistent-head set before detector evaluation and construct a strictly parameter-free score from prompt-time activations only—for example, the mean normalized projection of the persistent heads onto a harmful-versus-harmless direction exposed through the model’s native unembedding, with no learned probe, tuned lens, gradient updates, or response tokens. Evaluate clean and jailbroken harmful inputs from held-out AdvBench and JailbreakBench against benign Alpaca inputs, with deduplication from circuit discovery and separate reporting for ordinary and successfully jailbroken prompts. Report AUROC and AUPRC, plus F1, false-positive rate, and false-negative rate at a preregistered zero threshold; if a threshold is calibrated, report it separately so it is not presented as a wholly training-free result. Compare under the same input-only protocol with publicly available dedicated models such as Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, and a public HarmBench classifier, using bootstrap confidence intervals and a preregistered non-inferiority margin such as three AUROC points. Also fit a conventional linear probe as an explicitly trained ceiling: if the parameter-free readout is weak but the probe is strong, the representations persist but additional training is required. Performance within the non-inferiority margin, including on successful jailbreaks and with acceptable benign false positives, would support the full detector claim; strong separability only after probe fitting would reject the no-additional-training subclaim, and poor performance for both readouts would undermine persistence or practical accessibility. This experiment could be replaced by a public, leakage-controlled benchmark containing frozen activation scores and predictions from the same dedicated safety baselines, provided the purported direct readout was fixed before its test set and truly used no fitted parameters.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Direct before-and-after evidence that successful attacks leave a measurable safety or refusal-related signal in internal activations, rather than eliminating that signal throughout the model.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed representational analysis records per-head activations and projections for matched ordinary and successful-jailbreak inputs, and tests a probe trained only on ordinary harmful-versus-benign examples without refitting. This can establish whether safety-relevant information remains available during successful attacks. Measuring attention heads rather than every component is a scope difference, not a failure to answer the claim that the representations persist.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A validated, same-instruction paired set containing genuine refusal-to-success transitions, so attack effects can be separated from differences in the underlying harmful requests.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 retains ordinary/jailbreak pairs for the same instruction only when the ordinary prompt is refused and the jailbreak succeeds, using multiple harmful-prompt and attack sources and a calibrated success judge. That provides the essential within-pair contrast; the claim does not require the reference study's particular attack families or sample counts.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A component-level discovery and scoring procedure that identifies a small group with selectively reduced safety-related output and a complementary group that retains the signal, with stability checks and controls against arbitrary selection thresholds or generic large perturbations.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed circuit-discovery analysis uses several attribution/discovery routes, sparsity sweeps, data-split and attack stability requirements, and size-, magnitude-, and random-head controls. It can identify and validate functionally suppressed versus persistent heads without reproducing the reference's particular scoring statistic or cutoff.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A held-out causal intervention showing that suppressing only the candidate head subset increases harmful compliance, with dose dependence and controls for the generic effects of perturbing an equal number of heads.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 0 supplies the discovery split and candidate subset, while experiment 1 intervenes on held-out refused harmful prompts across a dose range, patches successful-jailbreak values, tests reverse restoration, and includes random, magnitude-matched, failed-jailbreak, and benign controls. These outcomes directly test causal sufficiency and distinguish head-specific effects from indiscriminate model damage.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that heads outside the selectively suppressed subset retain harmful-content or refusal-related signal during successful attacks, rather than the residual signal being an artifact of the selected heads alone.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiment measures every head and tests probes trained on ordinary harmful-versus-benign cases on successful jailbreak activations without refitting. Persistence of probe accuracy in most heads, together with concentrated suppression in only a small subset, directly establishes that other heads continue to represent harmful content during attack success. Selective suppression of those other heads is one possible route to this conclusion, not a requirement of the claim.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-resolved attribution that separates representation of the original harmful request from response to the jailbreak template, allowing the head-type difference to be distinguished from a simpler difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed paired recordings and per-head projections can reveal whole-prompt differences between the head groups, but they do not decompose those activations into original-request tokens and attack-template tokens. Consequently, an observed head difference remains compatible with several sensitivity explanations.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment isolates harmful-request-token contributions from attack-template-token contributions to test the mechanistic rival explanation.
Proposed experiment 0 uses matched prompts and per-head measurements but specifies no token-level attribution or source decomposition.
A whole-prompt activation difference can be caused by sensitivity to harmful content, sensitivity to the jailbreak template, or both.
Thus the proposed measurements get at the head distinction but do not discriminate the competing mechanisms.
A team running the proposed set would fail to learn whether the separation is specifically template-driven rather than a difference in sensitivity to the harmful request itself.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A genuinely training-free internal readout whose quality is tested on held-out clean and jailbroken inputs, compared with dedicated safety systems, and validated for transfer across a broad range of safety benchmarks, models, and architectural families.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 directly addresses the no-additional-training requirement with a frozen parameter-free score, evaluates successful jailbreaks and benign inputs, and compares performance with dedicated safety baselines using preregistered metrics and uncertainty. Its evaluation is materially narrower than the reference scope: it is centered on two proposed prompt benchmarks and at least two checkpoints, with no requirement for multiple architecture families or a broad battery of safety evaluations. It can establish competitiveness on its tested scope but leaves broad transfer ambiguous.
reasoning_chain: The reference experiment establishes both detector usefulness and external generalization across many safety benchmarks, models, and architecture families.
Proposed experiment 2 tests a fixed parameter-free readout and dedicated baselines, but only on the two specified prompt sources and the limited checkpoints carried over from experiment 0.
A strong result on those data can show local detector quality while failing to show that the readout transfers beyond that model family and benchmark construction.
Therefore the direct-readout and comparison questions are addressed, but the generalization component has weaker evidential force.
A team running the proposed set would fail to learn whether the detector's competitive quality generalizes broadly across models and safety-evaluation regimes.

sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests the central conjuncts: persistence of safety-relevant information, selective concentration of attack-related suppression, causal sufficiency of the selected subset, continued harmful-content decodability, and a parameter-free detector comparison. The remaining gaps concern mechanistic resolution and validation breadth rather than an untested core: it lacks a causal suppression test on the persistent head group, token-level separation of harmful-request and jailbreak-template contributions, and the reference's broad cross-architecture benchmark transfer. Thus it could support the claim on the tested scope, but would not establish the strongest general mechanistic and external-validity interpretation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Paired, network-internal evidence that safety-relevant information remains present during successful attacks rather than disappearing relative to the corresponding unattacked request.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiment records head-level refusal and harmfulness projections in matched ordinary and successful-jailbreak conditions and tests no-refit diagnostic probes on the successful attacks. Persistent out-of-distribution probe accuracy and retained refusal-associated activity would distinguish bypass from wholesale erasure. The use of a different representational readout and probe-based test is adequate for the claim that the information remains internally available.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A paired corpus of the same harmful instructions in refused and successful-jailbreak conditions, with enough attack and benign variation to isolate the attack effect from request-content differences.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible and robustness-checked procedure for assigning safety-related functional roles to individual heads and identifying a concentrated suppressed subset rather than relying on an arbitrary component choice.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiment combines component discovery and attribution methods with sparsity sweeps, split and attack stability requirements, and size- and magnitude-matched controls. It also measures projections onto calibrated harmfulness and refusal directions. These provide comparable discriminating power to a separately calibrated head-scoring and threshold-sensitivity instrument.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A held-out causal intervention that varies the strength and number of candidate-head interventions and compares them with matched controls, while measuring whether refusal changes into relevant harmful compliance rather than merely producing degraded output.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiment intervenes on discovery-split heads using held-out refused harmful instructions, includes a dose sweep and jailbreak-value patching, and compares against random, magnitude-matched, failed-jailbreak, unmodified, and benign conditions. It measures refusal, relevant compliance, output divergence, and benign-task degradation, and its reverse patch tests restoration of refusal. This directly tests causal sufficiency with stronger controls than are strictly necessary.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token-level decomposition that separately measures head-type responses to the original harmful request and to the added jailbreak template, so selective attack sensitivity can be distinguished from a pre-existing difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiment compares matched ordinary and jailbreak prompts, failed attacks, benign controls, and headwise attributions, but it does not state that contributions are decomposed by token into original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens. Because those token groups differ together between the ordinary and successful conditions, observed head-type differences could still reflect sensitivity to harmful content rather than selective response to the jailbreak template.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would substantially test the claim: it constructs the necessary paired successful-jailbreak cases, identifies a concentrated head subset, tests causal sufficiency with strong controls, checks persistence in other heads, and evaluates a genuinely fixed detector against dedicated safety models. It would nevertheless leave two material issues unresolved: the mechanistic rival explanation is not separated at the token level, and detector competitiveness is not validated across comparably diverse models and safety benchmarks. Thus it could support a scoped bypass account and scoped detector result, but would not fully settle the claim as stated.
